titlePl: Matura PR: Edukacja — 180 haseł do gier LingoSpark
titleEn: Matura Extended: Education — 180 terms for LingoSpark games
blurbPl: Dział Edukacja na maturę rozszerzoną: system oświaty, studia, ocenianie i uczenie się przez całe życie. Fiszki ENG–PL.
blurbEn: Extended Matura Education: school systems, university, assessment and lifelong learning.

items.definitionEn: a school funded by the government rather than by fees
items.example: Most pupils in England attend a state school near home.

items.definitionEn: a school funded by fees, not by the local authority
items.example: An independent school can set its own entrance exam.

items.definitionEn: in Britain, an old, expensive independent school
items.example: Eton is a famous public school, despite the confusing name.

items.definitionEn: a state secondary school that selects pupils by exam
items.example: She sat the eleven-plus to enter a grammar school.

items.definitionEn: a state secondary school that takes pupils of all abilities
items.example: The local comprehensive school does not select by test score.

items.definitionEn: a school where pupils live during term time
items.example: He boarded at a boarding school from the age of thirteen.

items.definitionEn: a school for only boys or only girls
items.example: Her parents chose a single-sex school for the sixth form.

items.definitionEn: a school that teaches boys and girls together
items.example: The old boys' college became a co-educational school in 1998.

items.definitionEn: a school linked to a religion and its values
items.example: The faith school requires a letter from the parish priest.

items.definitionEn: a school for pupils with significant additional needs
items.example: The special school has small classes and specialist staff.

items.definitionEn: a college that trains students for a trade or practical career
items.example: He left the liceum for a vocational college in catering.

items.definitionEn: the last two years of secondary school, often for A-levels
items.example: She stayed on in the sixth form to sit three A-levels.

items.definitionEn: study after secondary school that is not a full university degree
items.example: Further education colleges offer BTECs as well as A-levels.

items.definitionEn: a state-funded school in England that is independent of the local council
items.example: The failing comprehensive was turned into an academy school.

items.definitionEn: teaching pupils of different levels in the same class
items.example: Mixed-ability teaching can stretch stronger pupils if tasks are well designed.

items.definitionEn: putting pupils into classes by overall academic ability
items.example: Critics say academic streaming labels children too early.

items.definitionEn: the neighbourhood from which a school normally takes pupils
items.example: We moved house to get into a better school catchment area.

items.definitionEn: money paid to attend a private or independent school
items.example: School fees rose again above inflation this year.

items.definitionEn: a school that admits pupils by exam, interview or talent
items.example: Places at the selective school are fiercely competitive.

items.definitionEn: the years when the law requires children to be in education
items.example: Compulsory education in Poland lasts until eighteen.

items.definitionEn: a secondary school that combines general study with a trade
items.example: The technical school partners with local engineering firms.

items.definitionEn: subjects such as literature, history, philosophy and languages
items.example: She wants to study humanities rather than natural sciences.

items.definitionEn: subjects that study people and society, such as sociology or economics
items.example: Psychology sits between the social sciences and biology.

items.definitionEn: subjects such as physics, chemistry and biology
items.example: The faculty of natural sciences has a new laboratory wing.

items.definitionEn: a large division of a university grouping related departments
items.example: He applied to the faculty of law, not medicine.

items.definitionEn: a university unit that teaches and researches one subject
items.example: The academic department of chemistry runs evening lectures.

items.definitionEn: an outline of topics, texts and assessment for a course
items.example: Check the syllabus before you buy the set texts.

items.definitionEn: the official programme of study that state schools must follow
items.example: Citizenship was added to the national curriculum in the 2000s.

items.definitionEn: a subject all pupils must study, such as maths or the language of instruction
items.example: English remains a core subject until the end of secondary school.

items.definitionEn: a formal talk teaching a group, typical at university
items.example: The Monday lecture on ethics is always crowded.

items.definitionEn: a small class for discussion of a topic or text
items.example: Read the article before the seminar on Friday.

items.definitionEn: a very small teaching session, often with one tutor and a few students
items.example: Bring a draft essay to your tutorial.

items.definitionEn: practical experiments done in a science lab as part of a course
items.example: Twenty per cent of the mark comes from laboratory work.

items.definitionEn: research or practical study done outside the classroom, especially in geography
items.example: Geography fieldwork will take place on the coast in May.

items.definitionEn: a club or pursuit organised by the school but outside lessons
items.example: Debating is the extra-curricular activity that stretched her most.

items.definitionEn: practical preparation for a specific job or trade
items.example: Vocational training can lead to a skilled job without a degree.

items.definitionEn: a course that combines methods from more than one subject
items.example: The interdisciplinary course links ethics with computer science.

items.definitionEn: a preparatory year before a full degree, often for a change of field
items.example: Art students without A-levels take a foundation course first.

items.definitionEn: a British subject exam usually taken at eighteen for university entry
items.example: She needs AAB at A-level to keep her offer.

items.definitionEn: a British subject exam usually taken at sixteen
items.example: Most pupils sit GCSE maths and English.

items.definitionEn: a two-year diploma programme recognised by universities worldwide
items.example: The International Baccalaureate includes a core essay and community work.

items.definitionEn: the ability to read and write at a functional level
items.example: Adult literacy classes run at the local library.

items.definitionEn: the ability to use numbers in everyday and work situations
items.example: Poor numeracy holds people back in the labour market.

items.definitionEn: the skills needed to find, judge and use information, including online
items.example: Information literacy is now taught from the early years.

items.definitionEn: the grades or qualifications needed to join a course
items.example: The admission requirements include chemistry at a high grade.

items.definitionEn: a practice exam taken under real conditions before the official one
items.example: The mock exam showed she was weak on listening.

items.definitionEn: a second attempt at an exam after a fail or a low grade
items.example: He has a resit in August if he misses the pass mark.

items.definitionEn: assessed work completed during a course rather than in a final exam
items.example: The project counts as coursework and cannot be done overnight.

items.definitionEn: a spoken test of knowledge or language
items.example: The oral exam lasts twelve minutes with two examiners.

items.definitionEn: a formal test answered on paper or on screen
items.example: Mobile phones are forbidden in the written examination.

items.definitionEn: grading based on work throughout the course, not one final paper
items.example: Continuous assessment rewards steady effort rather than last-minute cramming.

items.definitionEn: checking progress to improve learning, often without a final grade
items.example: A quiz used as formative assessment need not go on the report.

items.definitionEn: a test or task that measures what has been learnt at the end of a unit
items.example: The June paper is the main summative assessment for the module.

items.definitionEn: the lowest score needed to succeed in a test
items.example: The pass mark was raised to fifty-five per cent.

items.definitionEn: the score at which one grade changes to the next
items.example: The grade boundary for an A shifted after the paper proved hard.

items.definitionEn: an official record of modules and grades from an institution
items.example: Attach your academic transcript to the master's application.

items.definitionEn: units that measure the workload of a course or module
items.example: You need 180 credit points to complete the bachelor's programme.

items.definitionEn: a person who supervises an exam to prevent cheating
items.example: The invigilator walked between the desks throughout the paper.

items.definitionEn: the organisation that sets and marks a public exam
items.example: Each exam board publishes its own past papers.

items.definitionEn: the stated standards used to award marks
items.example: Read the marking criteria before you write the essay.

items.definitionEn: students judging one another's work against shared criteria
items.example: Peer assessment works only if the checklist is clear.

items.definitionEn: judging your own work or skills against a standard
items.example: Self-assessment at the end of the unit showed gaps in grammar.

items.definitionEn: a test in which you may use notes or textbooks
items.example: An open-book exam still rewards those who have organised their notes.

items.definitionEn: to take a formal test
items.example: Candidates sit an exam in the sports hall in May.

items.definitionEn: the highest pass band on some courses and vocational awards
items.example: She completed the diploma with distinction.

items.definitionEn: a high pass band below distinction on some awards
items.example: A merit is enough to progress to the next year.

items.definitionEn: to formally ask for a mark to be reviewed
items.example: You may appeal a grade only on procedural grounds.

items.definitionEn: the result a teacher expects you to achieve in a public exam
items.example: Her predicted grade in biology is an A.

items.definitionEn: a published ranking of schools by exam results
items.example: Parents still hunt for the top of the school league table.

items.definitionEn: an exam given in the same way so scores can be compared
items.example: A standardised test cannot capture every kind of talent.

items.definitionEn: a short spoken report, often with slides, assessed for content and delivery
items.example: The oral presentation is worth ten per cent of the module.

items.definitionEn: to not reach the pass mark for a unit of a course
items.example: If you fail a module twice, you may have to leave the programme.

items.definitionEn: a university place that depends on achieving set exam grades
items.example: His conditional offer requires AAB including chemistry.

items.definitionEn: the British process matching leftover university places to students after results
items.example: She found a linguistics place through clearing.

items.definitionEn: the money charged by a university for teaching
items.example: Tuition fees have made some graduates wary of a master's.

items.definitionEn: money given to a student on merit or need to help pay for study
items.example: The scholarship covers accommodation as well as books.

items.definitionEn: the grounds and buildings of a university or college
items.example: Most first-years live on campus in the first term.

items.definitionEn: a student studying for a first degree, or that level of study
items.example: Undergraduate numbers rose after the new campus opened.

items.definitionEn: a student studying after a first degree, or that level of study
items.example: Postgraduate seminars meet in the research centre.

items.definitionEn: a long piece of original written work at the end of a degree
items.example: Her dissertation examines dialect change in Silesia.

items.definitionEn: an extended research text, especially for a master's or doctorate
items.example: He defended his thesis after three years of archival work.

items.definitionEn: a first academic degree, typically after three or four years
items.example: A bachelor's degree in engineering is the usual route into the firm.

items.definitionEn: a higher degree taken after a bachelor's, often one or two years
items.example: She funded the master's degree with a research bursary.

items.definitionEn: the highest university degree, awarded for original research
items.example: She is doing a PhD on bilingual education.

items.definitionEn: a first-year university student in Britain
items.example: Every fresher is assigned a personal tutor in week one.

items.definitionEn: university buildings where students live, often in the first year
items.example: Noise in the halls of residence peaks at the weekend.

items.definitionEn: money borrowed to pay fees or living costs while studying
items.example: A student loan is repaid only above a set income.

items.definitionEn: non-repayable help towards a student's living costs
items.example: The maintenance grant was means-tested and later cut.

items.definitionEn: money given by a school or university, often according to need
items.example: The college bursary paid for her rail season ticket.

items.definitionEn: a student who begins higher education later than the usual school-leaver age
items.example: As a mature student he brought ten years of workplace experience.

items.definitionEn: study done away from campus, typically online or by post
items.example: Distance learning let her finish the degree while working nights.

items.definitionEn: a mix of face-to-face teaching and online study
items.example: Blended learning reduced crowding in the lecture theatre.

items.definitionEn: an event when prospective students visit and ask questions
items.example: Go to an open day before you accept an offer.

items.definitionEn: a brochure or site describing courses, facilities and entry rules
items.example: The prospectus lists optional modules for year two.

items.definitionEn: to officially register on a course or at an institution
items.example: You must enrol in person before the first lecture.

items.definitionEn: a large sloping room designed for lectures
items.example: The lecture theatre holds four hundred students.

items.definitionEn: the teaching year at a school or university, not the calendar year
items.example: The academic year starts in October at this university.

items.definitionEn: a degree that includes a year of work in industry
items.example: The sandwich course placed him in a design studio for a year.

items.definitionEn: an arrangement to study for a time at a partner institution abroad
items.example: The exchange programme lasts one semester in Spain.

items.definitionEn: the academic head of a British university
items.example: The vice-chancellor spoke at the graduation ceremony.

items.definitionEn: the head of a faculty or a senior college officer
items.example: The dean approved her request to interrupt studies.

items.definitionEn: the lecturers, professors and researchers employed by a university
items.example: Academic staff went on a marking boycott last spring.

items.definitionEn: a formal article presenting original findings
items.example: Cite the research paper, not the newspaper summary.

items.definitionEn: a brief reference in the body of a text pointing to a source
items.example: Every in-text citation must match an entry in the bibliography.

items.definitionEn: the list of sources used in a piece of academic work
items.example: Put the bibliography on a separate page.

items.definitionEn: the highest UK bachelor's classification
items.example: First-class honours is rare in this department.

items.definitionEn: a degree that splits study equally between two subjects
items.example: Joint honours in history and politics kept both options open.

items.definitionEn: an extra preparatory year built into a degree for some students
items.example: The foundation year covers maths missing from her school course.

items.definitionEn: former students of a school or university
items.example: Alumni fund a hardship grant for current students.

items.definitionEn: the formal event at which degrees are conferred
items.example: Families travel far for the graduation ceremony.

items.definitionEn: the organisation that represents students and runs campus services
items.example: The students' union advised her during the appeal.

items.definitionEn: a member of staff assigned to support a student's academic progress
items.example: Email your personal tutor if you cannot submit on time.

items.definitionEn: the books and articles a tutor expects you to study
items.example: Start the reading list in the summer, not the night before.

items.definitionEn: published times when a lecturer is available to students
items.example: Office hours are Tuesdays from ten until twelve.

items.definitionEn: the staff member who guides a dissertation or research project
items.example: Meet your academic supervisor before you lock the title.

items.definitionEn: an oral examination, especially of a thesis
items.example: The viva voce lasted ninety minutes with two external examiners.

items.definitionEn: a period of supervised work that counts towards a course
items.example: The work placement is assessed by both the firm and the tutor.

items.definitionEn: the central service through which students apply to UK universities
items.example: You submit one personal statement through UCAS.

items.definitionEn: to study intensively in a short time before a test
items.example: Do not cram the night before a language oral.

items.definitionEn: memorising facts by repetition rather than by understanding
items.example: Rote learning will not help you in an unseen essay.

items.definitionEn: the skill of analysing arguments and evidence rather than accepting them
items.example: Critical thinking is assessed in every humanities paper.

items.definitionEn: using someone else's words or ideas as if they were your own
items.example: Plagiarism can mean failing the whole module.

items.definitionPl: rok przerwy (przed studiami lub w trakcie)
items.definitionEn: a year out of formal study, often used to travel or work
items.example: She took a gap year to work in a language school.

items.definitionEn: to leave a course before finishing it
items.example: Money worries made him drop out after the first term.

items.definitionEn: to miss lessons without permission
items.example: Students who skip classes fall behind within weeks.

items.definitionEn: to improve knowledge of something you used to know better
items.example: Brush up on your tenses before the oral exam.

items.definitionEn: to progress more slowly than the course or your peers
items.example: Miss two seminars and you will fall behind.

items.definitionEn: to reach the required level after being behind
items.example: She used the Easter break to catch up on labs.

items.definitionPl: zabrać się ostro do pracy / nauki
items.definitionEn: to start working seriously and with discipline
items.example: After the mock results he had to knuckle down.

items.definitionEn: to read quickly for the main points rather than every word
items.example: Skim-read the chapter first, then take notes.

items.definitionEn: a diagram of ideas branching from a central topic
items.example: A mind map helped her plan the argument.

items.definitionEn: a student who can plan, monitor and evaluate their own study
items.example: An autonomous learner does not wait to be told what to revise.

items.definitionEn: comments that explain how work can be improved, not only what is wrong
items.example: Constructive feedback on the draft saved the final mark.

items.definitionEn: planning study and rest so deadlines are met without last-minute panic
items.example: Poor time management, not ability, sank the project.

items.definitionEn: to delay work that should be done now
items.example: If you procrastinate until Sunday night, the essay will suffer.

items.definitionEn: a small set of students who revise or solve problems together
items.example: The study group meets in the library every Thursday.

items.definitionEn: an exam paper from a previous session, used for practice
items.example: Work through a past paper under timed conditions.

items.definitionEn: honesty in study, including proper citation and no cheating
items.example: Academic integrity rules cover collusion as well as copying.

items.definitionEn: to name the works you have used in academic writing
items.example: Always cite sources, even when you paraphrase.

items.definitionEn: to rewrite an idea in your own words while keeping the meaning
items.example: Paraphrase the critic, then add your own judgement.

items.definitionEn: to check a text for errors before submitting it
items.example: Proofread on paper; screens hide typos.

items.definitionEn: the maximum (and sometimes minimum) number of words allowed
items.example: The word limit is 1,500, not counting the bibliography.

items.definitionEn: a short summary of a paper or dissertation placed at the start
items.example: Write the abstract last, when the argument is stable.

items.definitionEn: learning difficulties or disabilities that require extra support in school
items.example: Special educational needs support can include extra time in exams.

items.definitionEn: a difficulty with reading and spelling that is not due to low intelligence
items.example: Dyslexia need not bar anyone from a literature degree.

items.definitionEn: a school student whose ability is well above the typical level
items.example: A gifted pupil still needs challenge, not only extra worksheets.

items.definitionEn: to do less well than your ability suggests
items.example: Able students underachieve when they are bored or anxious.

items.definitionEn: schooling that educates pupils with diverse needs in ordinary settings where possible
items.example: Inclusive education depends on trained staff, not slogans.

items.definitionEn: an ordinary school, as opposed to a specialist separate setting
items.example: Many deaf children now attend a mainstream school with support.

items.definitionEn: the habit of staying away from school without permission
items.example: Persistent truancy triggers a meeting with the family.

items.definitionEn: the knowledge and skills a course claims students will gain
items.example: Check the learning outcomes before you choose an optional module.

items.definitionEn: temporary help that is withdrawn as the learner becomes able to work alone
items.example: Scaffolding for the essay included a model paragraph and a checklist.

items.definitionEn: a teacher who covers classes when the regular teacher is absent
items.example: A supply teacher cannot be expected to know every pupil's target.

items.definitionEn: a member of staff who supports the teacher and individual pupils
items.example: The teaching assistant sat with the group that needed extra reading help.

items.definitionEn: the teacher in charge of a subject area in a school
items.example: The head of department moderated the coursework marks.

items.definitionEn: a teacher in the first year after gaining qualified teacher status
items.example: A newly qualified teacher has a reduced timetable and a mentor.

items.definitionEn: the skills of organising behaviour and attention so that teaching can happen
items.example: Classroom management is as demanding as subject knowledge.

items.definitionEn: removing a pupil from the school roll as a last disciplinary step
items.example: Permanent exclusion should be rare and carefully documented.

items.definitionEn: a temporary ban from attending school as a punishment
items.example: A five-day suspension followed the fight in the corridor.

items.definitionEn: a planned change to how schools, exams or funding work
items.example: Each education reform promised less paperwork and delivered more.

items.definitionEn: a lack of qualified staff to fill teaching posts
items.example: The teacher shortage is worst in physics and modern languages.

items.definitionEn: the number of pupils taught together in one group
items.example: Class size rose after two posts were left unfilled.

items.definitionEn: a method where students study content at home and practise in class
items.example: In a flipped classroom the lecture is a video watched beforehand.

items.definitionEn: a method in which pupils investigate questions rather than only receiving facts
items.example: Inquiry-based learning still needs a knowledgeable teacher.

items.definitionEn: study that uses digital platforms as the main medium
items.example: E-learning failed some pupils who had no quiet place to work.

items.definitionEn: a free or low-cost online course open to very large numbers of learners
items.example: He completed a MOOC on statistics before applying for the MSc.

items.definitionEn: continuing to study and retrain throughout adult life
items.example: Lifelong learning is no longer a slogan in a changing labour market.

items.definitionEn: organised learning for people who have left full-time school
items.example: Adult education classes in evening Polish fill every autumn.

items.definitionEn: ongoing training that keeps practitioners' skills up to date
items.example: Continuing professional development this year focuses on assessment.

items.definitionEn: designed around students' needs and activity rather than only the teacher's talk
items.example: A learner-centred lesson still has clear goals.

items.definitionEn: unfair differences in access, quality or outcomes of schooling
items.example: Educational inequality tracks family income more closely than talent.

items.definitionEn: the difference in exam results between groups of pupils
items.example: The attainment gap widened after lengthy school closures.

items.definitionPl: luka w dostępie do nauki w domu
items.definitionEn: unequal ability to study at home because of missing devices, internet or space
items.example: The homework gap showed up the first week of remote lessons.

items.definitionEn: growing up with fewer financial, educational or social resources
items.example: Outreach schemes target applicants from a disadvantaged background.

items.definitionEn: schooling that is highly selective, expensive or socially exclusive
items.example: Elite education still opens doors that grades alone do not.

items.definitionEn: the money provided to run schools, from the state or other sources
items.example: School funding per pupil has not kept pace with costs.

items.definitionEn: policies that help under-represented groups enter higher education
items.example: Widening participation is a condition of the university's public grant.

items.definitionEn: paid one-to-one or small-group teaching outside school
items.example: Private tuition in maths has become a hidden school fee.

items.definitionEn: the share of students who leave a course before finishing
items.example: The dropout rate is highest in the first undergraduate year.

items.definitionPl: dodatek na uczniów z trudniejszego środowiska
items.definitionEn: extra state money in England for schools with disadvantaged pupils
items.example: The pupil premium paid for a breakfast club and extra tutoring.
